Malleefowl nests, constructed as large incubation mounds of decomposing organic matter, rely critically on external temperature to regulate embryonic development. Eggs deposited within these mounds at a depth corresponding to approximately 34 °C [T = 34 °C] will hatch after an incubation period of about 62 days [ab = about 62 days], a duration that is highly sensitive to even minor thermal fluctuations. The hatchling emerges weighing approximately 114 grams [Wwb = approximately 114 grams], a substantial initial mass that provides a significant buffer during the first days of life as the chick begins to navigate its environment. This neonatal mass is considerably larger than that of many other galliform species, reflecting the extended period of development within the egg. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg itself is around 175 grams [Ww0 = around 175 grams], indicating a substantial investment of maternal resources into each individual offspring before any external feeding occurs. Field records show that mound temperatures can vary between 29 and 38 °C depending on the season and solar exposure.

Under the sustained thermal conditions that define the active metabolic period for adult Malleefowl, specifically at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], several key life-history milestones have been quantified. The growth trajectory of the newly hatched chick is remarkably rapid, with a weight increase at birth of 2.75 grams per day , allowing the bird to quickly increase its body mass and thermoregulatory capacity at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This rapid early growth is an adaptation seen in many precocial species, enabling the chick to become independent more quickly. These chicks reach a critical developmental stage known as puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation, at approximately 244 days since birth [tp = approximately 244 days since birth] under these same laboratory conditions at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This age at puberty is relatively early compared to the overall lifespan of the bird and marks the transition into the sub-adult phase. Some sub-adult birds have been recorded as young as 14 months.

Adult body size in Malleefowl shows a clear sexual dimorphism, with females achieving a lower asymptotic mass than males. Under optimal conditions, the ultimate wet weight for females stabilizes at approximately 1830 grams [Wwi = approximately 1830 grams], a figure that reflects the energetic demands of egg production and mound maintenance. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males is substantially higher, reaching about 2040 grams [Wwi = about 2040 grams], a difference that is likely linked to the physical demands of territory defense and mound construction. This size difference is modest in percentage terms compared to some polygynous species but is consistent within the genus. The attainment of this adult mass occurs after the period of rapid juvenile growth has concluded, signaling the completion of the somatic development phase. These values were compiled from a large series of museum specimens and field captures across the species range.

The first successful breeding event for a female Malleefowl typically occurs after a considerable period of growth and social maturation. The time since birth at first brood has been measured at approximately 1,278 days [tR = approximately 1,278 days] under the warm incubation conditions of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], a delay that reflects the time needed to reach full adult body size and to establish a suitable territory for mound construction. This relatively late onset of reproduction is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy. Once an adult female is reproductively active, her maximum reproductive rate is impressive. Field surveys indicate that a female will produce a single large clutch per year, containing an average of 18.6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 18.6 eggs per clutch], and a female typically produces one such clutch annually [F_R_i = one such clutch annually]. This represents a substantial annual investment of energy and calcium.

In the context of a K-selected life history, the Malleefowl exhibits a remarkable potential longevity. The maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals is approximately 7.5 years [am = approximately 7.5 years], a figure that allows for multiple reproductive seasons and underscores the species' investment in long-term survival at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This extended lifespan, combined with the relatively large clutch size, suggests that the species can withstand periods of low recruitment. However, the species also faces considerable environmental pressures. The need to maintain precise mound temperatures for egg incubation, such as the 34 °C [T = 34 °C] required for the 62-day incubation period (62 days) [ab = 62 days], makes it particularly vulnerable to climatic shifts that alter soil moisture and solar radiation. Conservation efforts are focused on preserving the mosaic of fire-prone and fire-excluded habitats that these birds require for their complex nesting behavior. Future research should examine how climate change will alter the thermal profile of these mounds and, consequently, the hatching success and early growth rates of chicks.
